method_ar: استمع كاملاً بلا نصّ. عمّا يتحدّث؟ قلها في جملة واحدة.
استمع مرة أخرى واكتب أي كلمة لم تلتقطها.

transcript.en: I have interviewed about four hundred people. The worst interview I ever conducted was not the candidate's fault, and I still think about it.
transcript.ar: أجريت مقابلات مع نحو أربعمئة شخص. وأسوأ مقابلة أجريتها لم تكن بسبب المتقدّم، وما زلت أفكّر فيها.

transcript.en: He was clearly nervous. English was his third language and he apologised for it in the first minute, which I told him was unnecessary. He answered the first two questions well.
transcript.ar: كان متوتّراً بوضوح. الإنجليزية لغته الثالثة، واعتذر عن ذلك في الدقيقة الأولى، فقلت له إن ذلك غير ضروري. وأجاب عن السؤالين الأولين إجابة جيدة.

transcript.en: Then I asked him a question with a phrasal verb in it. I said: "How do you go about solving a problem you've never seen before?"
transcript.ar: ثم سألته سؤالاً فيه فعل مركّب. قلت: «How do you go about solving a problem you’ve never seen before?»

transcript.en: He froze. I could see him working through the words. I should have rephrased it immediately, and I did not, because I was curious about what he would do.
transcript.ar: فتجمّد. رأيته يفكّ الكلمات في رأسه. وكان ينبغي أن أُعيد صياغة السؤال في الحال، ولم أفعل، لأنني كنت أريد أن أرى ماذا سيفعل.

transcript.en: What he did was guess. He talked for two minutes about going to different places, because he had understood "go about" literally. It was completely coherent and completely irrelevant, and by the end of it he knew.
transcript.ar: والذي فعله أنه خمّن. تحدّث دقيقتين عن الذهاب إلى أماكن مختلفة، لأنه فهم «go about» فهماً حرفياً. كان كلامه متّسقاً تماماً وبلا علاقة تماماً، وفي نهايته عرف ذلك.

transcript.en: He said: "I'm sorry — I think I misunderstood the question. Could you ask it in a different way?"
transcript.ar: فقال: «آسف — أظنّ أنني أخطأت فهم السؤال. هل تسأله بطريقة أخرى؟»

transcript.en: That was the moment he got the job. Not because the answer that followed was good, although it was. Because he had noticed, admitted it, and asked for what he needed — under pressure, in his third language, in front of a stranger.
transcript.ar: تلك هي اللحظة التي حصل فيها على العمل. لا لأن الجواب الذي تلاها كان جيداً، وإن كان جيداً. بل لأنه لاحظ، واعترف، وطلب ما يحتاجه — تحت ضغط، بلغته الثالثة، أمام غريب.

transcript.en: I have never once hired somebody for having perfect English. I have hired several people for being able to say "I don't understand" without falling apart.
transcript.ar: لم أوظّف أحداً قطّ لأن إنجليزيته كاملة. لكنني وظّفت أشخاصاً عدّة لأنهم يستطيعون أن يقولوا «لا أفهم» بلا أن ينهاروا.

payload.method_ar: اقرأ مرتين. الأولى بلا توقّف، والثانية مع المسرد.

story.en: A linguist counted how often people apologise in different countries. In Britain, the average person says "sorry" about eight times a day. Almost none of those are apologies.
story.ar: أحصى عالم لغة عدد مرات اعتذار الناس في بلدان مختلفة. في بريطانيا يقول الشخص العادي «sorry» نحو ثماني مرات في اليوم. ولا يكاد أيٌّ منها اعتذاراً.

story.en: They are something else. "Sorry" is used to interrupt, to ask a question, to disagree, to express sympathy, to move past somebody in a corridor, and — famously — when somebody else steps on your foot.
story.ar: هي شيء آخر. تُستخدم «sorry» للمقاطعة، ولطرح سؤال، وللمخالفة، وللتعاطف، وللمرور بجانب أحدهم في ممرّ، و— وهذا أشهرها — حين يطأ أحدٌ قدمَك.

story.en: Learners find this baffling, and they are right to. It is not politeness in the ordinary sense. It is a social signal that means roughly: "I am aware of you, and I am not trying to take anything from you."
story.ar: يجد المتعلّمون هذا محيّراً، ولهم الحقّ. فهو ليس أدباً بالمعنى المعتاد، بل إشارة اجتماعية معناها تقريباً: «أنا منتبه إليك، ولا أحاول أن آخذ منك شيئاً».

story.en: The same is true of "please" and "thank you", which appear far more often in English than in most languages, and of the enormous padding around requests. "I was wondering whether you might possibly have a moment" contains nine words before the actual question begins.
story.ar: والأمر نفسه في «please» و«thank you»، وهما أكثر وروداً في الإنجليزية منهما في معظم اللغات، وكذلك الحشو الهائل حول الطلبات. فعبارة «I was wondering whether you might possibly have a moment» فيها تسع كلمات قبل أن يبدأ السؤال الفعلي.

story.en: Speakers of languages that do not do this are frequently heard as abrupt when they speak English — not because of anything they said, but because of what they left out.
story.ar: والناطقون بلغات لا تفعل هذا يُسمَعون كثيراً حادّين حين يتكلّمون الإنجليزية — لا بسبب شيء قالوه، بل بسبب شيء تركوه.

story.en: The linguist's advice was practical. She said learners should over-use these words for the first year, because the cost of being slightly too polite is nothing, and the cost of being accidentally rude in an interview or a hospital is very high indeed.
story.ar: وكانت نصيحة عالم اللغة عملية: قال إنه ينبغي للمتعلّمين أن يُفرطوا في استخدام هذه الكلمات في السنة الأولى، لأن ثمن أن تكون مؤدَّباً أكثر من اللازم قليلاً لا شيء، وثمن أن تكون وقحاً بلا قصد في مقابلة أو مستشفى ثمن باهظ جداً.

payload.intro_ar: الأدب في الإنجليزية ليس في الكلمات وحدها بل في النغمة. الطلب نفسه بكلماته نفسها يكون طلباً مؤدَّباً أو أمراً جافّاً بحسب مدى صوتك وسرعته — وهذا ما يجعل المتعلّم يبدو حادّاً وهو لا يقصد.

payload.tip_ar: قل «Could you repeat that?» مرتين: مرة بنغمة مسطّحة سريعة ومرة بصعود ثم هبوط وأبطأ قليلاً. الكلمات واحدة، والأولى تُسمع مطالبةً والثانية طلباً.

sections.title_en: Break Time — English Outside the Book

payload.why_ar: كل ما سبق كان دراسة مكثّفة — كمّ قليل من اللغة يُفحص عن قرب. وهذا القسم مدخول موسّع: كمّ كبير من الإنجليزية يُستمتع به بتراخٍ. وأنت تحتاج الاثنين.
payload.rule_ar: قاعدة هذا القسم: **لا تدرسه**. لا تبحث عن كل كلمة، ولا تتوقّف لتحليل القواعد. اترك 40% يمرّ عليك. دماغك يبني الأنماط تحت السطح، وهذا العمل لا يحدث إلا حين تتوقّف عن المحاولة.
payload.how_much_ar: 20–30 دقيقة يومياً، **خارج ساعة الدراسة**. في السيارة، أو أثناء الطبخ، أو قبل النوم. هذا هو الجزء الذي لا يبدو عملاً — ولهذا بالضبط هو الجزء الذي يستمرّ عليه الناس فعلاً.
payload.links_note_ar: هذه مصادر حقيقية معروفة، لكن العناوين تتغيّر مع الوقت. لو لم يفتح رابط، ابحث عن الاسم — كل ما هنا يسهل إيجاده بالاسم.

text_en: Look at the first row. It is the only one that matters outside a classroom. If you completed all seven transactions — however imperfectly — you are functionally operational in English, which is what this entire course has been for.

blocks.heading_en: The Six Questions You Will Always Be Asked
head: Question
What they are really asking
Your structure
rows: Can you talk for ninety seconds without panicking?
Why do you want this job?
Have you thought about us at all?
What you know about them + what you want
Can you claim something without arrogance?
A real one + what you do about it
Tell me about a problem you solved.
Can you tell a structured story?
Do you have any questions for us?

blocks.text_en: "I'm a systems engineer. I've been at my current company for four years, mostly working on internal tools. // Before that I studied engineering in Cairo and spent two years at a smaller firm. // I'm looking for a role with more responsibility for the whole product rather than one part of it, which is why I applied here."
extra: The structure: now, then, why here. Ninety seconds maximum. Do not start with your childhood.

blocks.text_en: "I take on too much. If somebody asks me for help, I say yes before I've checked my own workload. // It caused a real problem two years ago when I missed a deadline because of it. // Now I keep a list of what I've committed to, and I look at it before I agree to anything. It hasn't happened again."
extra: *Never say "I'm a perfectionist" or "I work too hard".*** Interviewers hear these every day and they read as evasion. A real weakness plus a real fix is far more impressive than a fake weakness.

blocks.text_en: Always have two. These four are safe and useful in any interview:
extra: What does a good first six months look like in this role?
What is the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?
How would you describe the way the team works together?
Is there anything about my experience you'd like me to explain further?

blocks.text_en: Write five sentences for each of the six questions in §3.1. Not a script — five sentences. Then say each answer aloud three times and record the first two.

items.why_ar: أن تُقاطِع بأدب، وتخالف بلا خصومة، وتطلب التوضيح بلا حرج.

blocks.heading_en: The Four Things You Need To Do
head: Function
Phrases
rows: I think… / In my view… / From my side, the issue is…
Exactly. / That's a fair point. / I agree with Lina on this.
I take your point, but… / I'm not sure I agree. / I see it slightly differently.
Sorry, can I just add something? / Can I come in here? / Just one thing —

head: Situation
What to say
rows: You were interrupted and want to finish
Sorry — can I just finish my point?
You lost track of the discussion
Sorry, can we go back a step? What are we deciding exactly?
You need the decision written down
Just so we're clear — who's doing what by when?
You disagree with your manager in public
Can I offer a different view on that?
You need more time before committing
I'd rather look at the numbers before I commit.
You did not understand and it matters
Sorry, I want to make sure I follow — could you say that again?
You want to end your turn

blocks.text_en: **"Can we go back a step?" is worth memorising perfectly.** In a fast meeting in a second language you will lose the thread. That sentence buys you the whole context back, and nobody thinks less of you for asking.
Imagine a meeting about a decision at your work. Record yourself doing all four functions in §4.1 and three from §4.2, in a single two-minute stretch.

items.why_ar: رحلة ألغيت أو حقيبة ضاعت — خمس خطوات تُخرجك من الموقف.

blocks.text_en: Almost every travel problem follows the same five steps. Learn the sequence and you can handle any of them.

head: Step
What you say
Example
rows: State the problem in one sentence
Hello — I have a problem with my booking.
The reference is ABC123. Here's my passport.
The flight was cancelled and nobody contacted me.
What are my options? / Can you put me on the next one?
So, just to be clear — I fly at six from gate twelve?

head: Phrase
Arabic
Phrase
Arabic
rows: I'd like to change my booking.
Could I speak to a manager?

blocks.text_en: Step 5 is the one everybody skips and everybody needs. Repeat the outcome back in your own words before you walk away. Half of all travel disasters in a second language happen because somebody nodded at something they had not fully understood.
Role-play these three using the five-step sequence. Record the customer's side only.
extra: 1. Your flight is cancelled. The next one is tomorrow.
2. Your hotel has given your room to somebody else.
3. Your luggage has not arrived and you fly on again in two days.

items.why_ar: أصعب موقف: بلا وجهٍ ولا شفتين تقرأهما. عبارات تُنجيك.

blocks.text_en: The phone is the hardest situation in this chapter, because there is no face, no gestures and no lip movement — only sound.

blocks.heading_en: Why It Is Harder, and What To Do
head: The problem
The fix
rows: Ask for slower speech at the start, not after five minutes
Sorry, the line isn't very good. Could you say that again? — always available, always believable
Repeat every number back, digit by digit. Always.
You cannot ask them to write it
Could you send me that by email as well?
Use "Let me check" — it explains the silence

head: Stage
What to say
rows: Hello, this is [name] from [company]. Could I speak to …, please?
Could I leave a message? / When would be a good time to call back?
Can I take a message? … Let me read that back to you.
Sorry, the line isn't very clear — could you repeat that?
Could you spell that for me? — and use the letters: A for Alpha, B for Bravo.
So that's Thursday at ten, at your office. Is that right?

blocks.text_en: Have somebody read these aloud once, at speed. Write them down, then read them back.
extra: 15th of March        07700 900 461    Reference QX-4471
Numbers are the commonest point of failure on the phone, and they are also the easiest to fix — always read them back. Nobody has ever been annoyed by somebody confirming a number.

items.why_ar: أن تشتكي فتُحَلّ مشكلتك — لا أن تغضب فتُهمَل.

blocks.text_en: 1. SOFTEN     "I'm sorry to bother you, but..."
extra: 2. FACT       "I ordered this an hour ago."
3. PROBLEM    "It still hasn't arrived."
4. REQUEST    "Could you check what's happening?"
5. ESCALATE   "Is there somebody else I could speak to?"

head: Level
Phrase
When
rows: I'm sorry to bother you, but…
There seems to be a problem with…
I'd like to speak to a manager, please.
I'd like to make a formal complaint.

blocks.text_en: Start softer than you feel. English complaint culture escalates slowly, and starting at level four gets you treated as a difficult customer rather than a reasonable one. "I'm sorry to bother you, but…" opens far more doors than anger does — and you can always escalate afterwards.
Use the five-step formula for each. Record them.
extra: 1. Your food arrived cold, forty minutes late.
2. You were charged twice for the same thing.
3. Something you bought last week has already broken.

items.why_ar: طبيب أو شرطة أو تسريب ماء. تُقال بسرعة وبوضوح.

extra: WHERE   "On Nile Street, near the bank."
WHO     "One person. He's conscious but he can't walk."
YOU     "My name is Sami. My number is..."

In an emergency, grammar does not matter at all. Nouns and locations matter. "Accident. Nile Street. One man. Not walking." is a completely successful emergency call. Do not spend a second constructing a sentence.

items.why_ar: دقيقتان في مصعد أو انتظار. أسهل ما يُتعلَّم وأكثر ما يُخيف.

blocks.text_en: Small talk is the situation learners dread most, because there is no transaction to complete and no script. It is also the most learnable, because the topics never change.
Somebody asks you a question. Do THREE things:
extra: ANSWER  "Yes, I did."
ADD     "It took about an hour - the traffic was terrible."
ASK     "Did you come far?"
A one-word answer kills the conversation.
Answer + Add + Ask keeps it alive indefinitely.

This is the whole technique. Almost every failed conversation in a second language fails because the learner answers and stops. The other person then has to do all the work, and after three questions they give up. Answer, add, ask — three parts, every time.

blocks.heading_en: Exercise 6 — Two minutes with a stranger
blocks.text_en: Record a two-minute small-talk conversation, playing both parts. Use answer, add, ask at least five times, and finish with a polite escape.
